subject: ela
cluster: Research to build and present knowledge
skillName: Gather relevant information from multiple sources
intro: Each problem gives you a research question, one or two short sources, a source sentence, a citation, or a student version. Compare the choices, weigh credibility and relevance, judge paraphrasing and plagiarism, and decide when to quote or paraphrase. Everything you need is inside the problem. Write your answer and a short explanation.

items.prompt: Research question: 'Is the drinking water in Maple County safe?' Compare these two sources. Source 1: A report on the Maple County Health Department website (a .gov site), posted last month, that lists results from lab tests of the water. Source 2: A post in an online neighborhood group where one resident writes, 'My water tastes fine, so it must be safe.' Which source is more credible for answering the question, and explain why?
items.answer: Source 1 is more credible because it comes from an expert government agency, is recent, and offers tested evidence, while Source 2 is one person's opinion based only on taste.

steps: Check who wrote each source. Source 1 is the county Health Department, an expert agency; Source 2 is a single resident with no special expertise.
Check the evidence. Source 1 reports actual lab test results; Source 2 offers only a personal impression from how the water tastes.
Check the date and purpose. Source 1 was posted last month to inform the public; Source 2 is a casual opinion.
Because Source 1 has expert authorship, recent date, and tested evidence, it is the more credible source.

items.prompt: A student researching space writes from this source sentence: 'Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system.' Which of the following is an accurate paraphrase in the student's own words rather than a near copy? Option 1: 'Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system.' Option 2: 'In our solar system, Jupiter is the biggest planet of all.' Choose the better paraphrase and explain what makes it a paraphrase.
items.answer: Option 2 is the better paraphrase because it keeps the same meaning while changing the wording and sentence structure, instead of repeating the original almost word for word.

steps: Compare the meaning. Both options say Jupiter is the largest planet, so the meaning is preserved in each.
Compare the wording. Option 1 is identical to the source, so it is a copy, not a paraphrase.
Option 2 swaps 'largest' for 'biggest', adds 'of all', and reorders the sentence, so the words and structure are the student's own.
A true paraphrase keeps the meaning but uses new wording, so Option 2 is correct.

items.prompt: Original source sentence: 'Sea otters keep kelp forests healthy by eating the sea urchins that destroy them.' A student wrote: 'Sea otters keep kelp forests healthy by eating the sea urchins that wreck them.' The student did not use quotation marks or credit the author. Is this plagiarism? Answer yes or no and explain why.
items.answer: Yes, this is plagiarism because the student kept the original sentence structure and only swapped one word ('destroy' for 'wreck'), with no quotation marks and no credit to the author.

steps: Compare the two sentences side by side. Almost every word and the whole structure match the original.
The only change is replacing 'destroy' with 'wreck', which is changing just one word.
Swapping a few words while keeping the same structure is still plagiarism, not a real paraphrase.
Because there are no quotation marks and no credit, the borrowed sentence is plagiarized.

items.prompt: Research question: 'How does recycling aluminum cans save energy?' Compare two sources. Source A: 'Energy Savings from Recycling Metals,' an article on a university engineering department website that cites data on energy use. Source B: 'Buy Our Recycling Bins Today,' a company sales page that says its bins are the best. Which source is more relevant and credible for the question, and explain why?
items.answer: Source A is more relevant and credible because it directly addresses energy savings from recycling metals and comes from a university with cited data, while Source B is an ad meant to sell bins.

steps: Match each source to the research question, which is about energy saved by recycling aluminum.
Source A is about energy savings from recycling metals, so it is on topic; Source B is about selling bins, which does not answer the question.
Check purpose and evidence. Source A is from a university and cites data; Source B is an advertisement with a goal of selling a product.
Source A wins on both relevance and credibility, so it is the better source.

items.prompt: A student is writing a report and finds this exact statistic in a source: 'The Great Barrier Reef stretches more than 1,400 miles.' The student wants to include this precise number. Should the student quote it directly or paraphrase it, and what should the student do to use it correctly?
items.answer: Either can work, but because the exact number matters, quoting it directly with quotation marks and crediting the author is safest; a correct paraphrase such as 'The Great Barrier Reef is over 1,400 miles long' is also acceptable as long as the figure stays exact.

steps: Notice the source gives a precise statistic, the number 1,400 miles, which must stay accurate.
When exact wording or an exact figure matters, quoting word for word with quotation marks and credit is the safe choice.
A paraphrase is also allowed if it keeps the exact figure and changes only the surrounding words, such as 'is over 1,400 miles long'.
Either way, the student must keep the number exact and credit the source so it is not plagiarized.

items.prompt: Original source sentence: 'Most of the oxygen we breathe is made by ocean plants, not by trees.' Two student paraphrases are shown. Version 1: 'Ocean plants, rather than trees, produce most of the oxygen people breathe.' Version 2: 'Trees produce most of the oxygen we breathe, not ocean plants.' Which version is an accurate paraphrase, and explain what is wrong with the other one?
items.answer: Version 1 is the accurate paraphrase because it keeps the meaning that ocean plants make most oxygen; Version 2 is wrong because it reverses the meaning by saying trees make most oxygen.

steps: Read the original meaning: ocean plants, not trees, make most of the oxygen.
Check Version 1. It says ocean plants rather than trees produce most oxygen, which matches the original meaning.
Check Version 2. It says trees produce most oxygen, which reverses the original idea.
A paraphrase must keep the meaning, so Version 1 is correct and Version 2 changes the meaning.

items.prompt: Here is a complete citation: 'Maria Lopez. "Saving the Coral Reefs." Ocean Today. 2022.' A second citation reads: '"Saving the Coral Reefs." 2022.' Which bibliographic elements are missing from the second citation, and why do they matter?
items.answer: The author (Maria Lopez) and the source or website name (Ocean Today) are missing; they matter because a basic citation needs author, title, source, and date so a reader can find and trust the source.

steps: List the four basic citation parts: author, title, source or website, and date.
Check the second citation. It has the title and the date but no author and no source name.
Compare to the complete citation, which shows the missing author is Maria Lopez and the missing source is Ocean Today.
Without the author and source, a reader cannot locate or judge the source, so both are needed.

items.prompt: Research question: 'What caused the population of wild bees to decline?' Compare two sources. Source 1: A two-line note from a science museum site: 'Studies link bee decline to pesticide use and habitat loss. The findings come from researchers tracking hives over ten years.' Source 2: A one-line comment on a video: 'Bees are just lazy these days, lol.' Which source should the student use, and explain your reasoning?
items.answer: Source 1 should be used because it is relevant, comes from a science museum, and is based on a ten-year research study, while Source 2 is an unsupported joke that does not answer the question.

steps: Match each source to the question about why wild bees declined.
Source 1 names specific causes (pesticides and habitat loss) and is based on a ten-year study, so it is relevant and backed by evidence.
Source 2 is a joke with no evidence and does not actually explain a cause.
Source 1 has relevance, expert authorship, and evidence, so it is the source to use.

items.prompt: A student copies this sentence exactly from a source into a report: 'Volcanic ash can travel thousands of miles and disrupt air travel.' The student adds no quotation marks and does not name the author, but argues, 'It is fine because the sentence is true.' Is the student correct? Explain why or why not.
items.answer: No, the student is not correct; copying a sentence word for word without quotation marks and without crediting the author is plagiarism, even if the sentence is true.

steps: Identify what the student did: copied the sentence exactly with no quotation marks and no author credit.
A statement being true does not make copying it acceptable.
To use the exact wording, the student must put it in quotation marks and credit the author, or restate it as a real paraphrase.
Because neither was done, this is plagiarism.

items.prompt: Research question: 'How did ancient Romans build long-lasting roads?' Two sources are listed. Source A: 'Roman Road Engineering,' a history museum web page describing the layered materials Romans used. Source B: 'Best Road Trips Across Italy,' a travel blog listing scenic drives. Which source is more relevant to the question, and explain why the other one does not fit even though it mentions roads?
items.answer: Source A is more relevant because it explains how Romans engineered their roads; Source B only lists modern scenic drives and does not explain how the roads were built, even though it mentions roads.

steps: Reread the question. It asks how Romans built durable roads, so the answer must explain construction.
Source A describes the layered materials Roman engineers used, which directly answers the question.
Source B is about modern road trips and scenery, so mentioning roads is not the same as explaining how ancient roads were built.
Relevance depends on answering the question, so Source A is the correct choice.

items.prompt: Original source sentence: 'Honeybees communicate the location of flowers by performing a waggle dance.' A student wrote this paraphrase: 'Honeybees do a special dance to tell other bees where flowers are.' Is this an acceptable paraphrase or is it plagiarism? Explain your answer.
items.answer: It is an acceptable paraphrase because the student kept the meaning that bees use a dance to share flower locations but changed the wording and sentence structure into their own words.

steps: Compare the meanings. Both sentences say bees use a dance to show where flowers are, so the meaning is kept.
Compare the wording. The student replaced 'communicate the location of flowers' with 'tell other bees where flowers are' and 'performing a waggle dance' with 'do a special dance'.
The structure and most words are different, so this is not a near copy.
Because the meaning is preserved and the wording is original, it is a true paraphrase, not plagiarism.

items.prompt: Research question: 'Is it safe to swim at Cedar Beach this week?' Compare two sources. Source 1: A water quality alert from the county park service website (a .gov site) posted two days ago. Source 2: A travel article posted three years ago that calls Cedar Beach 'a lovely place to visit.' Which source is more useful for answering the question, and explain why date matters here?
items.answer: Source 1 is more useful because it directly reports current water safety and was posted two days ago, while Source 2 is three years old and only describes the beach as pleasant, not whether it is safe this week.

steps: The question asks about safety this week, so up-to-date information is essential.
Source 1 is a current water quality alert from the park service, which directly answers a safety question.
Source 2 is three years old and only calls the beach lovely, which does not tell you about safety now.
Because the question is about the present, the recent and on-topic Source 1 is more useful.

items.prompt: A student is writing about a famous speech and wants to include the speaker's exact memorable words: 'I have a dream.' Should the student quote these words directly or paraphrase them, and explain your choice.
items.answer: The student should quote the words directly with quotation marks and credit the speaker, because the exact, memorable wording matters and paraphrasing famous wording would lose its power and meaning.

steps: Decide what matters here. The words are famous and their exact phrasing is the point.
When the precise wording is important or memorable, quoting directly is the right choice.
Paraphrasing 'I have a dream' into other words would weaken or change the meaning.
So the student should quote it word for word with quotation marks and credit the speaker.

items.prompt: Original source sentence: 'The desert can be freezing cold at night even though it is very hot during the day.' Two student versions follow. Version 1: 'The desert can be freezing cold at night even though it is very hot in the day.' Version 2: 'Deserts often get very cold after dark, despite being extremely hot in the daytime.' One only swaps a word and is plagiarism; one is a real paraphrase. Identify each and explain.
items.answer: Version 1 is plagiarism because it keeps the original structure and only swaps 'during' for 'in', while Version 2 is a real paraphrase because it restates the idea with new wording and structure.

steps: Compare Version 1 to the original. It is nearly identical, changing only 'during the day' to 'in the day'.
Swapping one word while keeping the structure is plagiarism, not paraphrasing.
Compare Version 2 to the original. It uses new words like 'after dark' and 'in the daytime' and a new structure while keeping the meaning.
So Version 1 is plagiarism and Version 2 is an acceptable paraphrase.

items.prompt: Two citations for the same article are shown. Citation 1: 'Daniel Kim. "How Volcanoes Form." Science Daily. 2021.' Citation 2: 'How Volcanoes Form. Science Daily.' Which citation is more complete, and which bibliographic elements does the other one lack?
items.answer: Citation 1 is more complete; Citation 2 lacks the author (Daniel Kim) and the date (2021), and it also leaves the title without quotation marks.

steps: List the four basic parts: author, title, source or website, and date.
Check Citation 1. It includes the author, the title in quotation marks, the source, and the date, so it has all four parts.
Check Citation 2. It has only the title and source, so it is missing the author and the date.
Because Citation 1 has every required element, it is the more complete citation.
